subsection: 4. Case study: the Treaty negotiations, October–December 1921

notes.h: Background and causes: the Truce and the British offer, June–August 1921
notes.b: The War of Independence (1919–21) ended in a Truce, but a truce only stops the fighting. Months of talk and letters were needed before a formal conference could meet, and the central question was already clear: the Crown, meaning the British monarchy and Ireland's link to it.
points: The First Dáil (the Irish assembly set up by Sinn Féin) had declared a republic in January 1919, and the IRA owed its loyalty to the Dáil. This is why anything short of a republic was bound to be controversial.

Partition was already in place: the Government of Ireland Act 1920 had created Northern Ireland, with its own parliament and a unionist government under James Craig, and the talks had to deal with this existing border, which is why Ulster became one of the hardest issues.
George V called for reconciliation in his Belfast speech on 22 June 1921, and Lloyd George then invited de Valera to talks in a letter of 24 June. The Truce came into force at noon on 11 July 1921.
De Valera met Lloyd George in London four times in July 1921 (14, 15, 18 and 21 July), and neither side could shift the other on principle, so the talks produced no agreement.

The British proposals, handed over on 20 July, offered dominion status (self-government within the Empire, like Canada) with restrictions: British control of defence and the ports, free trade, and no change to the position of the six counties, which republicans saw as too restrictive for independence.

In August 1921 Ireland's government rejected the offer. De Valera's counter-proposal was ‘external association’: Ireland would be a separate state linked to the British Commonwealth, with the Crown recognised only as head of the association, not as ruler of Ireland.

notes.h: Background and causes: from correspondence to conference, August–October 1921
notes.b: After the offer was refused, both sides kept talking by letter. Each also had practical reasons to want a settlement, which is why the conference finally met.
points: Through the late summer Lloyd George insisted that Ireland accept the Crown and remain within the Empire, while de Valera insisted on the right of self-determination, that is, the Irish people's right to choose their own government.

Lloyd George's invitation of 29 September proposed a conference to see how the association of Ireland with the Empire might be reconciled with Irish national aspirations. The Irish accepted, and the conference opened at 10 Downing Street on 11 October 1921.

Britain wanted a settlement because the war was costing money and reputation, the dominion prime ministers urged compromise, and reconquest would have needed a very large army and martial law over the whole island.
The Irish side wanted a settlement because the IRA was short of arms and ammunition, and because civilians in the war zones were paying a heavy cost.
notes.tip: Exams ask why Britain and the Irish each wanted a settlement, so give a reason for each side, and keep external association (a separate state linked to the Commonwealth) distinct from dominion status.

notes.h: The delegations and the plenipotentiary issue
notes.b: Who went to London, and with what powers, shaped the outcome and the argument about it afterwards. De Valera chose to stay in Dublin, and the delegates carried two different sets of authority.
points: The Irish delegation was agreed in September 1921: Arthur Griffith (chairman), Michael Collins, Robert Barton, George Gavan Duffy and Éamonn Duggan.
Erskine Childers was the delegation's secretary, with Diarmuid O'Hegarty, John Chartres and others as assistant secretaries.
The delegation lived at 22 Hans Place in Knightsbridge, while Collins stayed separately at 15 Cadogan Gardens. Keep the two addresses apart: it matters when placing a document.
De Valera stayed in Dublin, saying that as head of state he should be held in reserve and that he had to keep republican opinion on side. Cathal Brugha and Austin Stack also stayed at home.

Critics, including Collins, argued that this was a mistake, because the man with most authority and most experience of Lloyd George was absent, and he later disowned the result, which is why the criticism was so sharp.
The delegates' credentials described them as plenipotentiaries, which meant they had full power to negotiate and sign a treaty without further approval.

Their written instructions were different: they were to submit the draft treaty to Dublin before signing and await a reply. How binding this was is still disputed, and it is the heart of the plenipotentiary issue, because full powers and a duty to refer back pulled in opposite directions.

The British team was Lloyd George (Prime Minister), Austen Chamberlain (Lord Privy Seal), Lord Birkenhead (Lord Chancellor), Winston Churchill (Colonial Secretary), Sir Laming Worthington-Evans (War Secretary), Sir Hamar Greenwood (Chief Secretary for Ireland) and Gordon Hewart (Attorney General).
Lionel Curtis and the cabinet secretary Tom Jones acted as advisers and go-betweens, carrying messages between the two sides.
notes.tip: A common exam angle is who negotiated and with what authority. Contrast the credentials (full powers) with the instructions (submit the final text to Dublin), and use the addresses to place a document.

notes.h: The negotiations: issues and sub-conferences, October–November 1921
notes.b: The conference began with full meetings of both sides but soon moved into small private groups, where Griffith and Collins argued with the British over four problems: the Crown, Ulster, defence and finance.
points: The plenary sessions (full meetings of both delegations) came early in the conference and produced no agreement. After that small sub-conferences met, with Griffith and Collins facing Lloyd George, Chamberlain and Birkenhead, so most of the bargaining was done privately, away from the full delegations.

The Crown and the oath: the British demanded an oath of allegiance (a promise of loyalty) to the Crown and membership of the Commonwealth, and the Irish tried to substitute external association and an oath to the constitution.
Ulster: the Irish argued that Ireland was one nation and that the six counties should not be allowed to opt out, because partition would divide the nation. Lloyd George said he could not coerce them.
The Boundary Commission idea came from the British side. Griffith and Collins took it as a way of removing large nationalist areas from the North, reducing it so much that it could not survive.
Defence: Britain insisted on naval facilities in Irish ports and coastal defence, which the Irish saw as a limit on their sovereignty (supreme power over their own affairs).
Trade and finance: the British wanted free trade between the two islands and a share of the British public debt, for example, while the Irish claimed offsetting counter-claims for overtaxation.

Craig and the Northern government refused to accept any all-Ireland arrangement, and Lloyd George, who had difficulty with the unionists, tried to extract concessions from Craig on the basis of a united Ireland within the Empire.
The delegates travelled to Dublin to consult the cabinet in November and December, so the process was not entirely independent of de Valera and the cabinet.
Throughout, Tom Jones and Lionel Curtis passed messages between Lloyd George and Griffith, and Collins formed a good relationship with Birkenhead.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to list the issues accurately: Crown and oath, Ulster and the Boundary Commission, defence and ports, finance and trade. Give one precise detail for each rather than a general description.

notes.h: The crisis and the signing, 1–6 December 1921
notes.b: The final week was a negotiation under deadline pressure. The decision to sign without sending the final text back to Dublin is the central controversy of the whole case study.
points: On 2 December Griffith privately assured Lloyd George that he would not let the conference break on Ulster, provided a Boundary Commission was set up. Lloyd George later treated this as a commitment, and republicans saw it as a concession made without the cabinet's knowledge.

On 3 December the delegates went to Dublin and met the cabinet. There was no agreement on the oath wording, and the delegates returned to London having been instructed not to accept the oath as drafted. So the delegates did consult Dublin, but not on a final text.

On 4 and 5 December the British pressed for signature. On 5 December Lloyd George said that refusal meant war, that he wanted a signature that night, and that his couriers were ready to carry letters to Craig either way.
Barton later recalled that Lloyd George warned of ‘immediate and terrible war’. Whether the threat was a bluff is still disputed.
The delegates returned to Hans Place, where Collins and Griffith argued that the alternative to signing was war. Barton, who had at first refused, gave way because he accepted that refusal meant war.

The Treaty (officially the Articles of Agreement for a Treaty between Great Britain and Ireland) was signed at 10 Downing Street at about 2.10 am on 6 December 1921 by all five Irish delegates, with the British team.
Collins afterwards wrote, in a letter of December 1921, that he had signed his own death warrant, a sign that he knew the Treaty would be bitterly resented, because it fell short of the republic.
De Valera was not told in advance. He learned of the signing on 6 December and was angry that the delegation had not sent the final text to Dublin.
notes.tip: For why the signing was controversial, give dated facts: Griffith's assurance of 2 December, the cabinet meeting of 3 December, the ultimatum of 5 December and the signing at about 2.10 am on 6 December. Do not say the delegates never consulted Dublin.

notes.b: The Treaty created the Irish Free State as a self-governing dominion in the Empire. It kept the Crown, an oath, British naval bases and partition, qualified by a Boundary Commission.
points: Article 1: the Irish Free State was to have the same constitutional status as Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and Newfoundland. This is dominion status, which falls short of a republic because the Crown remained, so republicans objected to it.

The Crown was represented in Ireland by a Governor-General, and the Free State's ministers were to be responsible to the Irish parliament, following Canadian practice, so real power rested with elected ministers and not the Crown.

The oath: members of the Free State parliament had to swear allegiance to the Constitution of the Free State and to be faithful to the King, ‘in virtue of the common citizenship of Ireland with Great Britain’.

Defence: Britain would defend the coasts and kept the use of the treaty ports (the naval harbours) of Berehaven, Queenstown (Cobh) and Lough Swilly, and of Belfast Lough, with the Free State army limited in proportion to population.
Finance: the Free State was to bear a share of the British public debt, subject to counter-claims, so Irish claims such as those for overtaxation could reduce the final sum.

Ulster: Northern Ireland could opt out of the Free State within one month of the Treaty's ratification, and a Boundary Commission would then settle the border ‘in accordance with the wishes of the inhabitants, so far as may be compatible with economic and geographical conditions’.
A Provisional Government would take over from the British administration until the Free State was established.
The Treaty had to be approved by the Dáil and by the British Parliament, and it was also to be ratified by a meeting of the House of Parliament of Southern Ireland.
notes.tip: Exams give marks for exact detail, so list the terms accurately: the dominion model, the oath, the ports, the one-month opt-out and the Boundary Commission. Do not confuse dominion status with de Valera's external association.

notes.h: The Dáil debates: cabinet, private sessions and public debate, December 1921–January 1922
notes.b: The Treaty still needed the Dáil's approval, and the debate that followed split the cabinet, the army and families, and led towards the Civil War.
points: On 8 December 1921 the cabinet divided four to three in favour of the Treaty. De Valera, Brugha and Stack were against.
De Valera issued a statement to the press saying that he could not recommend the Treaty to the Dáil.

The Dáil debated in private from 14 to 17 December. De Valera put forward his own alternative text, Document No. 2, based on external association. It was never presented to the British, so it was never a Treaty draft.
The public debate began on 19 December, was adjourned for Christmas and resumed in January 1922. Speakers included Griffith, Collins, Brugha, Mary MacSwiney and Childers.
Collins described the Treaty as giving ‘the freedom to achieve freedom’, a stepping stone to full independence, which is why he defended it, while Brugha attacked Collins's reputation.
Opponents argued that the oath and the Crown betrayed the republic proclaimed in 1916 and declared in 1919. Supporters argued that the people did not want more war.
All six women deputies voted against the Treaty.

notes.h: The Dáil vote and the new government, January 1922
notes.b: The vote decided the Treaty's fate, and the changes of government that followed put pro-Treaty leaders in power in Dublin and in the new Provisional Government.
points: The Dáil approved the Treaty on 7 January 1922 by 64 votes to 57. Do not confuse this with the cabinet vote of four to three.
De Valera resigned as President on 9 January and Griffith was elected President of Dáil Éireann on 10 January.
A Provisional Government under Collins was set up on 14 January and took over from the British administration when Dublin Castle was handed over on 16 January.
notes.tip: If asked how the Treaty led to the Civil War, link the split over the Crown, oath and partition, but add other causes such as army loyalties, personalities and the way the Treaty was negotiated.

notes.b: Griffith was chairman of the delegation and its senior negotiator. After the Treaty he led the pro-Treaty side in the Dáil until his early death.
points: Griffith (born 1871) was a Dublin printer and journalist who founded Sinn Féin in 1905. He advocated a dual monarchy, on the Hungarian model (two kingdoms sharing one king), and economic self-reliance.
He was arrested after the Rising, although he had not taken part in it, and in 1917 he stood aside for de Valera as Sinn Féin president.
He was acting head of the Dáil during de Valera's American tour in 1919–20 and was Minister for Foreign Affairs in 1921.

In London he led the negotiations on the Crown and Ulster, and he was prepared to accept dominion status within the Empire with the Boundary Commission. His letter of assurance of 2 December committed him on Ulster.
He was a shy, scholarly man, in poor health after months in prison, so the strain of the negotiations told heavily on him.
After his election as President of Dáil Éireann in January 1922 he led the pro-Treaty side until his death from a cerebral haemorrhage on 12 August 1922.
Contemporaries: supporters of the Treaty praised his courage and integrity, which is a judgement rather than a fact, while republicans condemned him as having abandoned the republic.
Historians stress his role in creating the political movement that won independence, through Sinn Féin, and his realism in 1921.
notes.tip: For a short paragraph on Griffith, give specific dated facts (Sinn Féin in 1905, stepping aside in 1917, chairman of the delegation, death on 12 August 1922) and a short judgement.

notes.h: Key personality: Michael Collins (role in the negotiations)
notes.b: Collins was reluctant to go to London, but his reputation as the man who had beaten the British gave the delegation influence and made it hard for the Dáil to reject the result.
points: Collins was Minister for Finance, president of the IRB (the Irish Republican Brotherhood, a secret republican organisation) and director of intelligence in the War of Independence.
He warned the cabinet that he would be a poor negotiator. He believed that his name was needed for the military side but that the politicians should lead, which explains why he went reluctantly.
In London he handled the military and financial issues and built relationships with Birkenhead and Churchill.
He accepted the Boundary Commission clause in the expectation that Tyrone, Fermanagh and parts of Armagh and Down would be transferred, and he believed Northern Ireland could not survive after that.
He argued on the night of 5 December that the IRA could not win another round and that the Treaty gave the means to build up the army and the state.
He saw the Treaty as giving ‘the freedom to achieve freedom’, so he signed it as a first step and not as the end.
He became chairman of the Provisional Government on 14 January 1922. His death in August 1922 belongs to the story of the Civil War.
Contemporaries: anti-Treaty republicans accused him of using his IRB position to override the cabinet, while his supporters said he was honest about the Treaty's limits.
Historians: Tim Pat Coogan sees him as a pragmatic realist, while Peter Hart draws attention to his ruthlessness.
notes.tip: For Collins, give what he did, why he signed (the Boundary Commission, the IRA's weakness, freedom to achieve freedom) and a dated fact, then add a short judgement.

notes.h: Key personality: Éamon de Valera (role in the negotiations)
notes.b: De Valera was President of Dáil Éireann, and his title was changed to President of the Republic in August 1921. He set the strategy and then rejected the outcome, and historians still argue about whether his decision to stay at home was shrewd or a mistake.
points: His talks with Lloyd George in July 1921 showed that the British would not allow an Irish republic, yet he remained committed to external association.
He chose the delegation and wrote its instructions, but did not join it. His reasons were to keep a power in reserve and to avoid committing the head of state.
He sent messages to London advising the delegates to hold out on the Crown and oath, and kept in touch with cabinet colleagues in Dublin.

After the signing he opposed the Treaty on the grounds that the delegates had signed without the cabinet's approval of the final text. He resigned as President on 9 January 1922 after the Treaty vote.
His Document No. 2 would have accepted the Crown as head of an association with the Commonwealth, with an oath to the constitution only. The Dáil did not adopt it.
Contemporaries: supporters of the Treaty said that he had set a trap for Collins and Griffith, and republicans said that he was upholding the Republic.

Historians: the Earl of Longford's Peace by Ordeal (1935) defended the delegates, while later writers such as Joseph Lee, Tim Pat Coogan and Diarmaid Ferriter see him as a politician who used ambiguity to hold the movement together.
notes.tip: On de Valera, balance what he did (July talks, choosing the delegation, staying home, Document No. 2) against a judgement: was staying in Dublin shrewd or a mistake?

notes.h: Assessment: significance and differing views of the Treaty
notes.b: Judgements depend on whether the Treaty is measured against the republic of 1916 and 1919 or against the realistic alternatives of December 1921. Weigh each claim against the other side's.
points: Achievement: Britain withdrew its army and administration from 26 counties, and the Free State got its own parliament, police, army and civil service.
Limit: the Treaty kept the Crown, the oath, British bases and partition, which republicans said betrayed the declared republic.
Pro-Treaty view: it gave the freedom to achieve freedom, and a refusal would have meant war in 1922 with the IRA short of arms.
Anti-Treaty view: the delegates were bullied into signing, and the Dáil had no right to give away the republic.
Public opinion: most newspapers, the Catholic bishops, farmers and business supported the Treaty, and pro-Treaty candidates won a clear majority in the June 1922 election.

Unionists saw the Treaty as removing the threat to the North, but the Boundary Commission disappointed nationalists in 1925, because it did not transfer the large areas Collins and Griffith had hoped for.
Later view: historians debate whether the delegates were out-manoeuvred, whether the ultimatum was a bluff, and whether de Valera's absence made a bad outcome more likely or was a shrewd move.
In the short term the Treaty split the movement and led to the Civil War. There is more on this in the Civil War.
notes.tip: Judgement answers need balance: Achievements against Limits, pro-Treaty against anti-Treaty, contemporary against later views. Back each side with a specific fact.

keyTerms.definition: Self-government within the British Empire on the model of Canada, which the Treaty gave the Irish Free State.
Loyalty owed to the Crown; the Treaty oath tied members of the Free State parliament to the Constitution and to the King.
Supreme power over a state's own affairs, which republicans said the Treaty limited with the Crown, the oath and British naval bases.
De Valera's proposal that Ireland be an independent republic associated with the Commonwealth, with the Crown recognised only as head of the association.
A negotiator with full power to act for his government, the status given to the five Irish delegates.
Berehaven, Queenstown (Cobh) and Lough Swilly, naval bases which Britain kept under the Treaty.
The commission the Treaty provided for to settle the border between Northern Ireland and the Free State.
The oath to the Constitution and faithfulness to the King required of members of the Free State parliament.
De Valera's alternative to the Treaty, put to the Dáil in December 1921 but never adopted.
The body chaired by Collins from 14 January 1922 that took over from the British administration before the Free State was formed.
